stress_tests.gate_compliance_60: 40% of people prop the gate or step around it
stress_tests.shortcut_40: 40% keep using the old route after a move
stress_tests.night_shift_inattention: Tired night shift: fewer people look

stress_why: The package introduces a pedestrian gate and shifts the crossing, but 40% of users are likely to bypass the gate entirely (gate_compliance_60), creating a new path that defeats the safety intent (shortcut_40). Additionally, the measured data shows a tag of 'proposed' and the controls rely on driver behavior; night_shift_inattention represents a high-risk scenario where tired operators fail to notice the relocated crossing or gate, directly threatening the 'ped_wait_s' and 'close_calls_per_shift' metrics.
revision_reasoning: The stress tests reveal that the 'Pedestrian gate only' package fails under gate_compliance_60 (22.7 conflicts/1000) and night_shift_inattention (13.5 conflicts/1000), both exceeding the 10.0 target. The 'Move crossing 3 m + pedestrian gate' package holds up under all three stress scenarios (max 11.1 conflicts/1000 under gate_compliance_60), but its upper bound of 11.1 slightly exceeds the target. The 'Move crossing 3 m + convex mirror + keep-clear marking' package fails catastrophically under shortcut_40 (25.7) and night_shift_inattention (56.3). No tested package robustly meets the 10.0 target under all stresses. A new package combining the moved crossing (which reduces blind-spot exposure) with the pedestrian gate (which enforces stop-and-look behavior) and a convex mirror (to further improve visibility at the new location) is needed to add redundancy and push the worst-case stress result below 10.0.
